metric_rationale: The experimental design carefully constructs trials such that Take The Best and Tallying always make strictly opposite predictions. By calculating the proportion of choices that are consistent with the Take The Best heuristic, we can perfectly separate the two theories: TTB will yield scores near 1.0, whereas Tallying will yield scores near 0.0.

This metric computes the proportion of choices that align with the Tallying heuristic. Tallying and Take The Best (TTB) make opposite predictions on 6 out of the 8 unique trial types in this design. Therefore, a subject using Tallying will have a high score on this metric (close to 1.0, depending on noise), whereas a subject using TTB will consistently choose the opposite on most trials, yielding a low score (around 0.25). Because the metric is an average over ~96 trials per subject, within-subject and between-subject variance will be low, easily distinguishing the two theories.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that favor the 'compensatory' option in trials where a single highly valid cue is opposed by multiple lower-validity cues (Trials 1, 2, and 4). Take The Best (TTB) will almost never choose the compensatory option because it strictly follows the first discriminating cue. Conversely, the Weighted Additive (WADD) model, depending on its non-linear scaling parameter gamma, will frequently choose the compensatory option as the combined weight of the lower-validity cues can outweigh the single best cue. This leads to a substantial difference in the expected value of this metric between the two theories.

In Trial 1 and Trial 3, Option A is favored by the single most valid discriminating cue, while Option B is favored by all remaining lower-validity cues. The Take The Best (TTB) model is non-compensatory and strictly follows the single best cue, so it will almost exclusively choose Option A (resulting in a response near 0). The Weighted Additive (WADD) model, however, integrates all cues; depending on its gamma parameter, the sum of the numerous lower-validity cues can outweigh the single best cue, leading to a much higher probability of choosing Option B. This metric isolates these highly compensatory trials and calculates the proportion of B choices, cleanly separating the two theories.

This metric exploits a perfect reversal in cue weighting between Linear WADD (used in Strategy Mixture) and Non-Linear WADD.

In Trial 8 (10011 vs 01100), Linear WADD sums raw validities and strictly favors Option A (2.06 vs 1.54). Since Take-The-Best (TTB) also favors A, the Strategy Mixture model predicts a very high P(A). In Trial 7 (11000 vs 00111), Linear WADD favors Option B (1.74 vs 1.86), opposing TTB. Consequently, the Strategy Mixture model's P(A) drops to roughly the mixture parameter 'alpha'. Thus, Strategy Mixture predicts P(A|T8) - P(A|T7) > 0.

In contrast, Non-Linear WADD transforms validities to log-odds. In Trial 7, Option A possesses the top two cues, which under log-odds scaling sum to a massive, insurmountable advantage over the bottom three cues for any gamma > 0. In Trial 8, Option B holds the strong second cue, making the contest much closer. Therefore, Non-Linear WADD predicts a stronger preference for A in Trial 7 than in Trial 8, yielding P(A|T8) - P(A|T7) < 0.

This robust sign flip clearly discriminates the two theories.

This metric calculates the difference in the rate of choosing the TTB-favored option between Trial 7 and Trials 3/6. Under the Competing theory (Strategy Mixture), the agent mixes between TTB and Linear WADD. In both Trial 7 and Trials 3/6, Linear WADD strongly favors the non-TTB option. Thus, the agent only chooses the TTB option when using the TTB heuristic, which happens with probability 'alpha'. Because 'alpha' is consistent, the difference in TTB choice rate between these trials is near 0. Under the Advocated theory (Non-linear log-odds WADD), the decision depends on the non-linear scaling of log-odds validities. In Trial 7, the log-odds of the TTB option's cues are strong enough to outweigh the opposing cues for ANY value of the scaling parameter 'gamma', leading to a consistently high TTB choice rate (~1.0). In Trials 3/6, the TTB option has only the top cue against all four other cues; for smaller values of 'gamma', the sum of the four non-TTB cues outweighs the top cue, pulling the average TTB choice rate down significantly. Therefore, the Advocated theory predicts a large positive difference.

This metric leverages a difference-in-differences approach to cancel out subject-specific variance. We isolate two groups of trials where Linear WADD opposes Take The Best (TTB). In Group 1, Log-Odds WADD agrees with TTB; in Group 2, Log-Odds WADD opposes TTB. Theory 1 (Strategy Mixture) mixes TTB and Linear WADD, so its probability of choosing the TTB winner is roughly the mixing parameter 'alpha' in both groups, yielding a difference near 0. Theory 2 (Cue Difference Threshold) relies on TTB but falls back to Log-Odds WADD. In Group 1, both TTB and the fallback strategy agree, leading to a high TTB choice rate. In Group 2, the fallback strategy opposes TTB, dragging the TTB choice rate down. Thus, Theory 2 predicts a substantially positive difference between the two groups, discriminating the theories cleanly.

By comparing trials where the log-odds WADD fallback favors the single-cue option (Group X) versus trials where the log-odds WADD fallback flips to favoring the multiple-cue option (Group Y), we can heavily penalize Theory 1's fallback mechanism. Theory 1 will show a massive drop in the rate of choosing the single-cue option from Group X to Group Y. Theory 2 uses linear WADD as its compensatory mechanism, which strongly favors the multiple-cue option in BOTH groups, meaning its choice probabilities will be much more stable across these two sets of trials.

In Theory 1 (Strategy Mixture), choices on disagree trials are a probabilistic mixture of TTB and WADD. Because both strategies are locally highly deterministic on these trials, the probability of choosing the TTB-favored option is simply the mixture parameter 'alpha', regardless of whether the first or second cue discriminates. Thus, Theory 1 predicts the TTB match rate will be identical across Group 1 and Group 2, making the difference ~0. 

In Theory 2 (Rank-Dependent Tallying), the decision relies on the difference in weighted tallies. When Cue 0 discriminates (Group 1), the score difference is massive (e.g. ~0.65), leading to a high TTB match rate. However, when Cue 0 is tied and Cue 1 discriminates (Group 2), the weight of Cue 1 (0.25) barely exceeds the sum of the remaining cues (0.2135), resulting in a tiny score difference (0.0365). Because Theory 2 uses a softmax rule, this tiny difference pushes the choice probability very close to 50%. Thus, Theory 2 predicts a drastically lower TTB match rate in Group 2 compared to Group 1, yielding a strongly positive difference.

Theory 1 operates as a strict non-compensatory (TTB-like) model due to its high gamma parameter, meaning it will only deviate from TTB choices due to random lapse (epsilon). Theory 2 mixes TTB with a compensatory WADD strategy, actively preferring the WADD-favored option when the two strategies disagree. This metric computes the probability of choosing the WADD-favored option on disagreement trials (Trials 1-6) and subtracts the empirical baseline lapse rate computed from agreement trials (Trials 7-8). For Theory 1, this difference will be ~0, while for Theory 2 it will be significantly positive (reflecting the WADD mixture component).
